1.title: The Great Hanoi Rat Hunt
1.teaser: How a bounty on rat tails left colonial Hanoi with more rats, not fewer.
story: In 1902 the French colonial government in Hanoi had a problem it had partly made for itself. The new sewers beneath the European quarter were meant to show off modern hygiene, but they had become ideal places for rats to breed: dark, sheltered and free of predators. Plague was moving through the region, and rats carried the fleas that spread it. The rats had to go.

In April the city hired Vietnamese rat-catchers to go down into the tunnels. The daily counts climbed into the thousands, and on one day in June more than 20,000 rats were reported killed. It still wasn’t enough. So the authorities opened the hunt to everyone, paying a small bounty for each rat. To spare officials from handling the bodies, a severed tail counted as proof.

Before long, people noticed rats running about with no tails. Hunters were catching rats, cutting off the tails and letting the animals go, so they would breed more rats and more bounties. Investigators later found rat farms in villages outside the city, raised purely for their tails, and tails were being brought in from across the region. The bounty was abandoned. The rats stayed.

In 1975 the economist Charles Goodhart, writing about British monetary policy, described the pattern underneath: ‘Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.’ The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later gave it the form most people quote: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. A tail was a decent sign of a dead rat right up until people were paid per tail.

Once you know it, you see it wherever a number stands in for the thing we actually care about: waiting times, exam results, response times, attendance figures. The number is never the point. Forget that, and someone, somewhere, starts farming tails.
1.takeaway: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Reward a number and people will find the cheapest way to move it, which is rarely the thing you wanted.

rabbitHole.title: Tails, cobras and cash for ash
rabbitHole.intro: The rat hunt is the cleanest example of a pattern that turns up wherever people are paid, praised or judged by a number. Here’s how far down it goes.

levels.heading: The cobra that probably never was
body: The best-known version of this story isn’t about rats. In the ‘cobra effect’, British officials in Delhi supposedly paid a bounty for dead cobras, locals bred cobras to claim it, the scheme was scrapped, and the breeders released their now-worthless snakes, leaving more cobras than before. The German economist Horst Siebert gave it the name in a 2001 book, Der Kobra-Effekt.

The trouble is the evidence. No contemporary record of cobra farming for a bounty has turned up, and the tale seems to rest on an unconfirmed allegation. Hanoi is different: the historian Michael Vann found the rat hunt documented in French colonial archives. There’s an irony here. A story about bad evidence spread because it was a good story.

levels.heading: Campbell’s law and the classroom
body: Working independently, the American psychologist Donald Campbell reached the same conclusion from the other direction. In a 1979 paper he wrote that ‘the more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.’

His example was schools. Achievement tests, he argued, can be useful indicators of how pupils are doing when teaching aims at general competence. But when test scores become the goal of teaching, they lose their value as indicators and distort education itself. Anyone who has watched a school chase a single headline figure will recognise the shape of it.

levels.heading: Cash for ash
body: Northern Ireland’s Renewable Heat Incentive, launched in 2012, paid businesses for every unit of heat produced by renewable boilers. The flaw was that the payment was worth more than the fuel. The more you burned, the more you earned.

Whistleblowers reported buildings that had never been heated being heated for the subsidy, including an empty farm shed. Fears of an overspend of up to £490 million over twenty years, a figure later disputed, fed a political crisis. On 9 January 2017 Martin McGuinness resigned as deputy First Minister, bringing down the Stormont Executive. The public inquiry that followed, chaired by Sir Patrick Coghlin, blamed a long run of errors and a failure of attention.

2.title: The Horse Who Could Count
2.teaser: A Berlin horse who did arithmetic, a panel of experts who were fooled, and the student who worked out what was really going on.
story: In the early 1900s, crowds in Berlin gathered to watch a horse do sums. His owner, Wilhelm von Osten, was a mathematics teacher who had spent years schooling him. Ask Hans a question and he would tap out the answer with his hoof. He could, apparently, add, subtract, multiply and divide, work with fractions, tell the time and spell out words.

In 1904 a panel of thirteen experts led by the psychologist Carl Stumpf examined Hans and found no sign of trickery. That wasn’t surprising. Von Osten wasn’t a showman; he sought no profit and sincerely believed he had taught his horse to think.

Stumpf passed the case to a psychologist named Oskar Pfungst, who ran a series of careful tests. The crucial one was simple: ask questions to which the questioner didn’t know the answer. Hans fell apart. When the person asking knew the answer and Hans could see them, he was right 89 per cent of the time. When they didn’t, he was right 6 per cent of the time. With blinkers on, he couldn’t answer at all.

Hans wasn’t counting. He was reading people. As a questioner bent forward to watch the hoof, Hans began to tap. When the count reached the right number, the questioner relaxed and lifted their head ever so slightly, and Hans stopped. Nobody was doing it on purpose: not von Osten, not the experts, not the crowd. Even Pfungst, once he knew exactly what to look for, had to make a conscious effort not to send the signals himself.

Psychologists now call this the Clever Hans effect. Our expectations leak out in signals too small for us to notice, and those signals shape the very thing we’re observing. It’s why careful experiments are run ‘blind’, so that whoever takes the measurements doesn’t know which result they’re hoping for. Hans really was clever, just not at arithmetic.
2.takeaway: What we expect leaks out in signals too small to notice, and those signals shape what we then see. To find out what’s really there, make sure whoever is checking doesn’t know what they’re hoping to find.

recall.question: Why did paying a bounty for rat tails leave colonial Hanoi with more rats?
recall.answer: Hunters cut off the tails and released the rats to breed, and some farmed rats purely for their tails. It’s Goodhart’s law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

rabbitHole.title: Expectations that leak
rabbitHole.intro: Pfungst’s horse became one of psychology’s most useful warnings. Follow it down and it leads to laboratories, classrooms and police dogs.

levels.heading: Bright rats, dull rats
body: In the early 1960s the psychologist Robert Rosenthal handed students some laboratory rats. Half the students were told their rats had been bred for brightness; the other half were told theirs had been bred for dullness. In reality there was no difference between the rats.

The students who believed they had bright rats got better learning out of them in mazes and Skinner boxes. Their own reports suggested they handled their animals more, and more gently. When the ‘dull’ group were told the truth, some insisted that their rat really was dull.

levels.heading: Pygmalion in the classroom
body: Rosenthal then took the idea into a school. With the principal Lenore Jacobson he told teachers that about a fifth of their pupils, actually picked at random, were about to bloom intellectually. A year later those pupils had gained about 12 IQ points on average, against about 8 for the rest. The effect showed up mainly in the youngest classes. The 1968 book Pygmalion in the Classroom made it famous.

It also drew decades of criticism. A major 2005 review by Lee Jussim and Kent Harber concluded that self-fulfilling prophecies in classrooms are real but usually small, and that teachers’ expectations mostly predict results because they are accurate rather than because they cause them. The most interesting exception: the effects may be larger for low-achieving pupils from poorer backgrounds and for stigmatised groups. That finding still needs replicating, but it suggests expectations may matter most for the pupils who are easiest to underestimate.

levels.heading: The dogs that read their handlers
body: In 2011 researchers at the University of California, Davis tested 18 certified police detection-dog teams. Handlers were told some of the search rooms contained target scent marked with a piece of red paper. In fact there was no target scent anywhere, so every alert was false.

The handlers called 225 alerts, and 85 per cent of runs included at least one. The alerts clustered where the red paper was, not where the researchers had hidden sausages and a tennis ball to tempt the dogs. The handlers’ beliefs shaped the result more than the dogs’ own noses. Pfungst would have recognised it at once.

3.title: The Ending Hemingway Left Out
3.teaser: Why Hemingway cut the most dramatic thing in a story, and why it made the story stronger.
story: In 1923 Ernest Hemingway was a young American newspaper correspondent based in Paris, not yet famous and determined to write fiction. One of his early stories, ‘Out of Season’, follows a young couple staying in Cortina d’Ampezzo in the Italian Alps. The husband hires the hotel’s drunken gardener, Peduzzi, as a fishing guide. Nothing goes right. Peduzzi wants money for drink, the wife is fed up, they’ve forgotten the lead weights and can’t fish. They agree to try again early next morning. On the way back Peduzzi asks for more money, and the husband pays, knowing he won’t see him again.

That’s all. But Hemingway knew something the reader doesn’t. Years later, in A Moveable Feast, he explained that he had ‘omitted the real end’, which was that the old man hanged himself. He cut it, he said, on his ‘new theory that you could omit anything if you knew that you omitted and the omitted part would strengthen the story and make people feel something more than they understood.’

In 1932, in Death in the Afternoon, he gave the idea the image that stuck: ‘The dignity of movement of an ice-berg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water.’ A writer who truly knows his subject can leave things out, and the reader will still feel them. But he added a warning people tend to forget: ‘A writer who omits things because he does not know them only makes hollow places in his writing.’

He put the theory to work. ‘Big Two-Hearted River’ follows a young man, Nick Adams, alone on a fishing trip: walking, making camp, cooking, casting. Hemingway said the story was about a boy coming home from the war, yet the war is never mentioned. In ‘Hills Like White Elephants’, a couple wait for a train in Spain and talk around an ‘operation’ that is never named. Readers have argued for nearly a century about what lies beneath both, and that is the point.

The iceberg is a bargain between writer and reader. The writer does the knowing; the reader does the feeling. Spell everything out and the reader has nothing to do. Leave the right thing unsaid and they supply it themselves.
3.takeaway: Leave out what you know, never what you don’t. A truth the writer fully understands but doesn’t state can be felt more strongly than one spelled out, because the reader has to supply it.

recall.question: How did Clever Hans the horse know when to stop tapping his hoof?
recall.answer: He read tiny, unconscious cues from the questioner, such as a slight lift of the head as the right count was reached. When nobody he could see knew the answer, he failed. That’s the Clever Hans effect.

rabbitHole.title: Beneath the waterline
rabbitHole.intro: Omission is a powerful tool, and powerful tools get misused and misremembered. Here’s where the idea came from, what happened when someone else held the knife, and the most famous example Hemingway never wrote.

levels.heading: The moon in a broken bottle
body: Writers are often told ‘show, don’t tell’, usually with a line credited to Anton Chekhov: ‘Don’t tell me the moon is shining; show me the glint of light on broken glass.’ Chekhov never wrote it. The researchers at Quote Investigator could find no sign of that compressed version before 2002.

What he did write, in a letter to his brother Alexander in May 1886, was advice on describing nature through small details. You get the full effect of a moonlit night, he said, if you write that on the mill dam a piece of glass from a broken bottle glittered like a bright little star. It’s the same instinct as the iceberg: choose the one detail that lets the reader build the rest.

levels.heading: The editor with the knife
body: Raymond Carver became famous in 1981 for a collection of startlingly spare stories, What We Talk About When We Talk About Love. Much of that spareness came from his editor, Gordon Lish. Lish cut the book by more than half. Three stories lost at least 70 per cent of their length, ten got new titles and fourteen got new endings.

On 8 July 1980 Carver wrote begging Lish to stop production, saying he was ‘mortally afraid’ the edited book might stop him writing another story. Less than a week later he wrote that he was thrilled about it. After Carver’s death, his original versions were published under the title Beginners. Read side by side, they raise Hemingway’s question: if someone else does the leaving out, whose iceberg is it?

levels.heading: Six words Hemingway never wrote
body: ‘For sale: baby shoes, never worn.’ The story goes that Hemingway wrote it to win a bet, and it is often called the perfect iceberg. There’s no evidence he wrote it.

Quote Investigator traced its ancestors to small ads in American newspapers: ‘For sale, baby carriage; never been used’ appeared in 1906. Writers spotted the story hiding in such ads well before the Hemingway version was in print. The anecdote attaching it to him appears in the 1980s and 1990s, long after he died in 1961. The best example of his theory is one where the author himself was left out.
